Adult somatic stem cells can divide indefinitely and are capable of generating various types of
cells via two types of cell division.
Symmetric division, in which somatic stem cells replicate and create more somatic stem cells.
Asymmetric division, producing a stem cell and a progenitor cell, which differentiates into a
particular type of cell.

Adult Somatic Stem Cells
The musculoskeletal system plays a diverse and key set of roles, from facilitating
mechanical leverage to serving as organ scaffolding and protection for thoracic contents.
Skeletal formation occurs early during embryologic development, and developmental
aberrations lead to multifactorial pathology. This process involves a cascade of events
facilitated by a series of cellular players. Whether the cells involved synthesize cartilage
or mineralize osteoid, all are linked by ancestral stem cells. Knowledge of such cells is
key in understanding not only biologic development but also the foundations of wound
healing and innovative therapeutic modalities.
Stem cells play crucial roles in embryologic musculoskeletal development because they
are the primordial origin of all agents involved in skeletogenesis, including osteoblasts,
osteocytes, mesenchymal cells, chondroblasts, and osteoclasts (Figure 1). After the initial
stage of embryologic development, localized populations of adult stem cells persist
throughout the body in regions where cellular replenishment will be required.

Populations of adult stem cells are immersed in unique microenvironments—stem-cell
niches—that influence their eventual cellular fate. At baseline, these stem-cell
populations maintain themselves through symmetric cellular division, during which one
stem cell gives rise to two identical daughter stem cells. Adult stem cells may be
mobilized to action in response to molecular, cellular, or physical stimuli. When this
mobilization occurs, an asymmetric form of cellular division happens, in which an adult
stem cell produces one daughter stem cell and another daughter progenitor cell. This
progenitor cell has limited replicative potential and may itself divide to further amplify
the production of downstream effector cells. In the context of connective tissue, this

asymmetric division gives rise to an admixture of stem cells and undifferentiated
progenitors, together termed connective tissue progenitors (CTPs), that may be
mobilized to facilitate recovery after insult.1
The niches of adult stem cells and their applications in orthopaedics are important.
Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs), hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), and their progeny
cells are involved in bone maintenance and repair. Physiologic stimuli responsible for
initiating stem-cell differentiation and the biologic signaling cascades are crucial for the
determination of adult stem-cell fate. Embryonic stem cells are possible therapeutic
agents, and research on induced pluripotency is ongoing.
MSCs and Their Derivatives
CTPs derived from the mesodermal germ layer that can differentiate into chondrocytes,
osteoblasts, fibroblasts, tenocytes, adipocytes, and myocytes
MSCs have been identified in various locations, including bone marrow, the periosteum,
adipose tissue, the umbilical cord, and amniotic fluid.
Activation of key transcription factors and genes induce differentiation.
Members of the sex-determining region Y-box family (SOX5, SOX6, and SOX9) are major
regulators of chondrocyte differentiation. Runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2)
induces chondrocyte hypertrophy.
RUNX2 and Osterix (Osx) are major transcription factors that induce osteoblast
differentiation. Wingless (Wnt) signaling also plays a crucial role.
Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARg) is the key transcription factor in
adipocyte differentiation.
Scleraxis (SCX) induces differentiation into tenoblasts/tenocytes.
MSCs have been investigated for therapeutic roles in the repair and regeneration of bone,
tendon, and cartilage.

MSCs are mesoderm-derived CTPs primarily localized within the bone marrow and
adipose tissue. Among CTPs, MSCs have garnered substantial interest for potential
cellular therapy applications because of their ability to differentiate into numerous cell
types and in multitudes. Exosomes derived from MSCs also have shown therapeutic
potential.2 A number of orthopaedic preclinical studies have been performed to manage
pathology ranging from cartilaginous repair to nonunion and metabolic disorders of the
bone.3 Various cell lineages derived from MSC are pertinent to orthopaedics, specifically,
chondroblasts/chondrocytes, osteoblasts/osteocytes, adipocytes and, tenoblasts.
Chondroblasts and Chondrocytes

Chondroblasts and Chondrocytes
Chondroblasts are cells that produce cartilaginous matrix and arise from MSCs.4,5
Chondroblasts differentiate from early chondroprogenitor cells into hypertrophic
chondrocytes, which continue to secrete cartilaginous matrix. This matrix then calcifies
to yield mineralized tissue.4 Most chondroprogenitor cells involved in endochondral
bone formation are localized to the central cartilaginous anlagen; however, some remain
on the proximal and distal ends of bones and differentiate into articular chondrocytes
involved in joint protection.4
Chondrocyte differentiation occurs via two distinct pathways: endochondral ossification
within bones and chondrogenesis within articular cartilage. During the process of
endochondral ossification—which forms the long bones of the appendicular skeleton
during development and continues with longitudinal growth from the physes until
skeletal maturity is attained—and fracture healing, cartilage anlagen serves as structural
scaffolding as chondrocytes undergo maturation, hypertrophy, and apoptosis.4,5 The
second pathway of chondrocyte differentiation is exclusive to hyaline cartilage. These
chondrocytes remain relatively quiescent, to lend structural, load-bearing, and force-
absorbing properties to joints.5

Chondrogenesis commences with the accumulation of mesenchymal tissue, forming
anlagen, comprised of extracellular matrix-secreting and collagen-secreting cells
surrounded by matrix constituent molecules, such as aggrecan and the alpha 1 chain of
type II collagen.6 Chondrocyte differentiation and the appropriate secretion of
extracellular matrix in time and space are regulated by the interaction of numerous
morphogens and growth factors and their receptors, which activate various signaling
pathways, resulting in the expression of specific transcription factors.6 SOX9 is
upregulated in early development and further modulated by the activation of myriad
other signaling pathways for chondrogenesis.5,7,8 A key player in these pathways, the
morphogen Sonic hedgehog, interacts with the transmembrane receptors Patched 1 and
Patched 2 for the mediation of chondrogenesis and chondrocyte hypertrophy.8,9
Signaling through Patched 1 and Patched 2 results in the recruitment of the
transmembrane protein Smoothened and activation of glioma-associated transcription
factors.10 This process results in the downstream upregulation of NK3 homeobox 28 and
further activation of SOX9.11
Notch is a system of four transmembrane receptors with distinct intracellular,
extracellular, and transmembrane domains that contributes to a reduction in
chondroprogenitor cell differentiation into chondrocytes via transcriptional regulation of
SOX9.7 After activation by agonist ligands including Delta-like 1, 3, and 4 and Jagged 1
and 2, receptor activation inhibits SOX9 via the Notch-activated transcription factor
recombination signal binding protein for immunoglobulin kappa J region and
downstream activation of regulators, such as hairy enhancer of split-1 and hairy
enhancer of split-5.7 Chondrogenesis is crucially dependent on reduced signaling
through the Notch pathway and, therefore, the relieved transcriptional repression of
SOX9.7
After the salvage of SOX9 signaling after the repression of Notch, the expansion of
chondrogenesis and chondrocyte hypertrophy is mediated by fibroblast growth factors,
local hypoxia, and upregulation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha and transforming
growth factor beta.12-14 Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) belong to the
transforming growth factor beta superfamily and are highly chondrogenic.14 The BMP
signaling blockade hinders cartilage formation via overexpression of the decoy receptor

Articular chondrocytes are formed from interzone cells and persist into adulthood.
Articular cartilage is present in the form of four distinct cellular zones running from the
synovial surface to the bone and consists of superficial, intermediate, radial, and
calcified cartilage, respectively. In the superficial zone, one to two cell layers of flattened
chondrocytes express proteoglycan 4, SOX9, type 2 collagen, aggrecan, and tenascin
C.5,16 Within the intermediate zone, round chondrocytes display similar expression
profiles as the cells of the superficial zone, with the exception of proteoglycan 4, and
lower levels of cartilage intermediate layer protein.16 Finally, radial and calcified layer
chondrocytes express chondrocyte differentiation and hypertrophy markers, including
type X collagen.5,16

Articular cartilage begins to develop at the synovial joints during embryogenesis via a
sequence of local patterning, interzone formation, cavitation, and morphogenesis.5,16
The four zones of articular (hyaline) cartilage are maintained throughout adulthood,
unless homeostatic signaling mechanisms are disrupted by traumatic injury,
inflammation of any cause, or genetic defects.16 In addition, maintenance of these
signals is required to avoid terminal hypertrophy of chondrocytes in synovial joints. The
major signaling pathway that suppresses this hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation is
transforming growth factor beta/small + mothers against decapentaplegic.17 Disruption
of this pathway results in increased expression of matrix-degrading enzymes, such as
matrix metalloproteinase-9 and metalloproteinase-13 and enzymes within the A
disintegrin and metalloprotease with thrombospondin motifs family.18 Degenerative
joint diseases, such as osteoarthritis, result from a concurrent, progressive loss of load-
bearing articular cartilage matrix and terminal chondrocyte maturation, resulting in type
X collagen secretion and chondrocyte apoptosis.5,18
Numerous two-dimensional and three-dimensional culture conditions support
chondrocyte differentiation.5 Type II collagen is the predominant extracellular matrix
protein in cartilage. The other major component of the extracellular matrix is
proteoglycan, which includes proteins containing covalently bound glycosaminoglycan
chains, such as aggrecan, with chondroitin sulfate and keratin sulfate side chains.5,18
Proteoglycans confer unique mechanical properties to cartilage, such as the ability to
absorb repetitive compressive mechanical loads without incurring joint damage.16,18
Numerous chondrocyte phenotypic markers are specific to chondrocyte differentiation,
such as the expression of type X collagen exclusively by hypertrophic chondrocytes.18
Chondroprogenitor cells committed to differentiation along this pathway also express
high levels of alkaline phosphatase, in contrast to noncommitted progenitor cells with
minimal levels of alkaline phosphatase.18 Chondrocytes committed to progression along
the endochondral ossification pathway express and respond to growth factors such as
BMPs and Indian hedgehog and parathyroid hormone (PTH)-related protein, which
inhibits chondrocyte maturation via inhibition of RUNX2.5,9,19,20 The differential
expression of these chondrogenic genes in articular cartilage, epiphyseal plates, and
sites of fracture healing highlights the critical regulatory role of various genes and
transcription factors in determining chondrocyte phenotypes. A summary of key factors
involved in chondrogenesis is provided in Table 1.

Osteoblasts work alongside chondrocytes and play crucial roles in endochondral and
intramembranous ossification (Figure 3). Differentiation to mature osteoblasts is a
complex, multistage process (Figure 4). It incorporates actions performed via multiple
pathways, most notably the RUNX2 transcription factor, the Wnt-ß-catenin signaling
pathway, and the Osx transcription factor.21 Each of these pathways is related to
osteoblast maturation. A summary of factors involved in osteoblastogenesis is provided
in Table 1.

RUNX2 is a transcription factor essential for osteoblast differentiation. Murine research
has highlighted the key role RUNX2 plays in osteoblast production and calcification.
Across two studies, heterozygote knockout mice lacking RUNX2 possessed abnormal
calvarium formation, and homozygous knockouts lacking RUNX2 displayed completely
absent bone calcification, dying after birth.22 Conversely, mice overexpressing RUNX2
outside of the skeleton exhibited ectopic calcification.23 Additional research has
demonstrated that a series of key genes involved in bone metabolism are targeted by
RUNX2. They include receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B ligand (RANKL),
osteopontin, bone sialoprotein, osteocalcin, and osteoprotegerin (OPG).24 RUNX2
deletion in vascular smooth muscle resulted in diminished vascular smooth muscle

interaction with hypoxia-inducible factor-1alpha in the hypoxic environment of nascent
bone development. Together, RUNX2 and hypoxia-inducible factor-1alpha promote

A crucial element controlling the expression of RUNX2 is glucose. Before the expression
of RUNX2 in osteoblast precursors, the cells express the glucose transporter, glucose
transporter type 1, on their cellular membranes.25 The intake of glucose permitted by
this transporter impedes AMP-activated protein kinase-dependent degradation of the
RUNX2 complex, which facilitates osteoblast maturation. In addition, RUNX2 upregulates
the expression of glucose transporter type 1, thereby creating a positive feedback loop
in the presence of an adequate glucose supply.25
The Wnt family consists of a series of paracrine-signaling glycoprotein molecules that are
secreted into the extracellular environment. Multiple Wnt pathways exist, but the Wnt-ß-
catenin pathway is crucial to the process of osteoblast differentiation and osteogenesis.
In this pathway, Wnt binds with Wnt ligand, and the resulting Wnt-Wnt ligand complex
adheres to the G protein-coupled receptor, Frizzled, which is present on the surface
membrane of osteoblast progenitors.26 After this receptor complex associates with low-
density lipoprotein receptor-related protein (LRP) 5 and 6 co-receptors, it elicits the
release of ß-catenin from a protein complex that would otherwise lead to the
degradation of ß-catenin. After, ß-catenin accumulates within the cytoplasmic space,
where it eventually translocates across the nuclear envelope and serves as a
transcription factor.26 Translocation of ß-catenin results in the transcription of multiple
osteogenic genes, including RUNX2.21 Highlighting the integral role Wnt-ß-catenin plays,
genetic studies have shown that gain-of-function mutations in LRP5 resulted in
otosclerosis, whereas inactivating mutations in LRP5 resulted in osteoporosis-
pseudoglioma syndrome.

in completing osteoblast differentiation. Before Osx can contribute to osteoblast
development, osteochondroprogenitors first must be primed by RUNX2.27 This detail is
supported by the finding that mice embryos lacking Osx exhibit absent osteoblast

Bone primarily consists of type I collagen that has been ingrained with calcium and
phosphate in the form of hydroxyapatite.30 Osteoblasts lay the extracellular groundwork
for bone and facilitate bone mineralization. Typically, osteoblasts are situated at the
border of the extracellular matrix, particularly within the periosteum and endosteum,
and deposit bone in balance with osteoclastic resorption. This homeostasis adjusts to
alterations in blood serum ion concentration and physical stressors, such as fractures
and stress load. Aberrations in this equilibrium contribute to various bone pathologies.
Synthesis of the organic phase of bone, osteoid, is the foundation by which osteoblasts
begin their involvement in osteogenesis. Osteoid is comprised predominantly of type I
collagen (approximately 90%) and an amalgamation of glycosaminoglycans,
proteoglycans, and glycoproteins, which comprise ground substance.31 Osteoblasts
secrete procollagen, a type I collagen precursor that is modified sequentially within the
extracellular space and eventually gives rise to the meshwork of type I collagen that
comprises bone. Outside the osteoblast, procollagen undergoes posttranslational
modification via transpeptidases, forming tropocollagen. Individual tropocollagen
molecules are cross-linked to each other via lysyl oxidase. This structure stabilizes the
collagen complex and produces a nest-like construct of interlocking, triple-helical type I
collagen fibers.31 Interspersed among the type I collagen fibers are small quantities of
type III collagen and type IV collagen, which control fibril diameter.31,32 In addition to
serving as the structural framework for hydroxyapatite-based crystal deposition, this
collagen meshwork has a net effect in conferring structural integrity to bone by
increasing its elasticity and resistance to compressive force.
Although ground substance and other minute components comprise a comparatively
small constituent of osteoid, they confer substantial structural benefits to bone. The
glycoproteins osteocalcin, osteopontin, and osteonectin constitute most of the

Osteoblastic function is modulated via a series of hormonal influences that are affected
by serum ion concentrations. Osteoblasts express the cytoplasmic vitamin D receptor
which, if complexed with vitamin D, initiates the transcription of genes modulated by
vitamin D response elements.37 Osteoblasts possess various genes featuring vitamin D
response elements within their promotor sequence, particularly osteocalcin and
osteopontin, and vitamin D exerts a net influence of increased bone mineralization.38
PTH plays key roles in calcium homeostasis and dictates osteoblast function. PTH1
receptors are G-protein receptors present on the surface of osteoblasts and incite
osteoblasts to secrete RANKL.39 Because of their capacity to influence bone metabolism,
vitamin D and PTH analogues are used in orthopaedics.40,41 Another routinely employed
medication group, corticosteroids, also influences bone health. Corticosteroids directly
diminish osteogenesis by initiating proapoptotic pathways within osteoblasts.42
Osteocytes

Osteocytes
After osteoblasts complete their role in bone formation, they may undergo apoptosis,
become inactive, or ensconce themselves in bone and transition into osteocytes.43 The
specific details surrounding this range of alternatives remain poorly understood;
however, osteocytes express high levels of cytoskeletal proteins as they mature, and
their dendritic processes extend before mineralization.43 In vitro evidence suggests that
the physical nature of the extracellular matrix plays a role in osteocyte differentiation.44

Loss-of-function mutations in Osx and dentin matrix acidic phosphoprotein 1 result in
pathology characterized by poor formation of osteocytes.27,45
Osteocytes are found almost entirely entrapped within mineralized matrix. Narrow
passageways termed canaliculi snake their way through bone, and osteocyte dendrites
wind their way through the passages. These canaliculi connect osteocytes with
osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and other osteocytes and facilitate intercellular communication
via gap junctions bridging cell membranes and paracrine signaling.46 Osteocytes are
thought to play a role in maintaining the delicate homeostatic balance between
osteoblasts and osteoclasts. Evidence suggests that osteocytes have the capacity to
detect fluid pressure changes within canaliculi networks and may dictate osteolysis and
osteoblastic processes according to structural need.47,48 One osteocyte-specific
messenger, sclerostin, is a secretory protein inhibitor that diminishes osteoblastic bone
formation.49 This task is accomplished via the antagonism of LRP5 and the disruption of
the Wnt signaling cascade crucial for osteoblast development.
Adipocytes

Adipocytes
Adipocytes differentiate from multipotent MSCs via a complex series of intermediates
that are not well-characterized and are difficult to isolate.50 Two main phases of
adipogenesis exist: determination and terminal differentiation. Determination involves
pluripotent stem-cell commitment to adipocyte lineage via conversion to a preadipocyte,
which can no longer differentiate into other cell types.50 During terminal differentiation,
the preadipocyte develops the characteristics of mature adipocytes, including the
cellular components for lipid transport and synthesis, sensitivity to insulin, and the
production and secretion of adipocyte-specific proteins.50 Crucial transcription factors
involved throughout this process include PPARg and CCAAT-enhancer binding
proteins.50

PPARg, a member of the nuclear receptor superfamily, is the primary regulator of
adipogenesis because it is necessary and sufficient for this process to occur.50-52
Induced PPARg expression subsequently induces adipocyte differentiation in fibroblasts
and myoblasts, and no transcription factor capable of promoting adipogenesis in the
absence of PPARg has been discovered.53,54 In addition, signaling pathways critical to
adipogenesis have been found to converge on the regulation of PPARg expression
and/or activity. PPARg exists and acts within adipogenesis as two protein isoforms,
PPARg1 and PPARg2, which are produced via alternative splicing and promoter
activation.50 The relative roles of these isoforms in adipogenesis have yet to be fully
elucidated. PPARg also is required for the maintenance of the differentiated
preadipocyte state in a manner so important that dominant-negative mutations in
PPARg introduced to mature adipocytes may cause de-differentiation and adipocyte
death.55,56 In addition, the temporal expression of members of the CCAAT-enhancer
binding protein family during adipogenesis supports adipogenesis but may not be

On fertilization of an ovum, the resulting zygote is totipotent (capable of differentiation
into any cell present within the body). Over the next several days, the zygote divides
several times, each division growing the cellular population exponentially. By the time
mitotic division has yielded a total of 16 cells, the zygote transforms into a roughly
spherical structure called a morula. Approximately 120 hours after fertilization,
continued differentiation and cavitation within the morula produces a cellular bilayer
structure, the blastula, surrounding a hollow center, the blastocoel. The exterior cellular
lining of the blastula is composed of trophoblasts, cells that will further differentiate and
eventually give rise to placental tissues. Conversely, the cells lining the inner cavity of the
blastula are collectively termed the inner cellular mass.
The inner cellular mass consists of pluripotent embryonic stem cells. Unfortunately, the
isolation of embryonic stem cells involves destruction of the embryo, which explains the
controversy surrounding the use of embryonic stem cells. Several intrinsic properties of
embryonic stem cells suggest a great capacity for experimental and therapeutic value. As
pluripotent cells, embryonic stem cells may differentiate into tissue from all three germ
layers (ie, endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm). The embryonic stem cell-derived tissue
then may be used to differentiate into innumerable target lineages. In addition,
embryonic stem cells may undergo sequential culturing while retaining their genetic
integrity and intrinsic pluripotency. In most cells, division involves the gradual shortening
of terminal chromosomal regions, which diminishes the integrity of the genetic code
because successive replicative cycles may involve the deletion of crucial genetic material;
however, in embryonic stem cells, telomerase activity enables the addition of redundant
nucleotides at the chromosomal termini, thereby preventing the degradation of valuable
genetic material and enabling long-term clinical utility after a cell line has been obtained
(Figure 6).

Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are an artificially derived form of pluripotent stem cells.
Viral transduction is used to induce differentiated adult cells to undergo retrograde evolution
into stem cells via stem–cell-associated genes.
Stem-cell–associated genes include SOX2, octamer-binding transcription factor 3/4, MYC
proto-oncogene (c-Myc), Krüppel-like factor 4, and others. These genes are important for the
self-renewal aspects of pluripotent stem cells and for inducing pluripotency.

parallels that have been observed for these two types of cells are cell-doubling time,
embryoid-body formation, teratoma formation, and chromatin methylation patterns.

Partly because of the religious and ethical controversies surrounding embryonic stem

with sufficient sample size, produces cellular derivatives exhibiting newfound
pluripotency and self-renewal.92 However, because of the stochastic nature of
reprogramming, the production of iPSCs occurs between 0.1% and 0.8% efficiency across

various regulatory gene expression patterns in common with tumors, even

neoplasms occurring after patients received unproven stem-cell therapeutic
transplantation.97-99 For future therapeutic applications, most stem-cell differentiation is
planned to have occurred before transplantation into patients, theoretically limiting the
risk of developing neoplasia secondary to stem-cell transplantation; however, research
has shown that pluripotent derivatives still may possess malignant potential.96 Given
